clinicalPearls: A distinct oculorenal syndrome combining acute tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis, most often in adolescent girls and young women.
The uveitis is typically bilateral, non-granulomatous and anterior, though intermediate and posterior involvement can occur.
Ocular inflammation may precede, coincide with or, most commonly, follow the renal disease, so uveitis can be the presenting feature of occult nephritis.
Systemic prodrome of fever, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia and myalgia is common and helps flag the diagnosis.
Urinary beta-2 microglobulin is a sensitive marker of tubular injury and is characteristically elevated.
Renal features include a raised creatinine, sterile pyuria, low-grade proteinuria, glycosuria and features of tubular dysfunction.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, syphilis, Sjögren syndrome and other systemic causes of oculorenal disease must be ruled out.
The nephritis is usually managed with systemic corticosteroids and often recovers, whereas the uveitis tends to be chronic or relapsing and may need prolonged topical and steroid-sparing therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome is believed to be an immune-mediated, likely T-cell driven, hypersensitivity disorder in which a shared autoantigen or cross-reactive immune response targets both the renal tubulointerstitium and the uveal tract. The kidney shows an acute interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils with tubular injury, sometimes with non-caseating granulomata, producing tubular dysfunction and a rise in creatinine. A parallel immune response in the eye generates non-granulomatous uveitis. Cell-mediated immunity, circulating autoantibodies against a modified C-reactive protein found in both renal tubular cells and uveal tissue, and genetic susceptibility through certain HLA associations have all been implicated. Preceding drug exposure or infection may act as a trigger in susceptible individuals.
additionalDifferentials: sarcoidosis with renal and ocular involvement
drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis with separate uveitis
granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other ANCA-associated vasculitis
ocular tuberculosis or syphilis with renal disease
additionalInvestigations: serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate
urinary beta-2 microglobulin and urinalysis for sterile pyuria, glycosuria and proteinuria
renal biopsy showing acute tubulointerstitial nephritis when the diagnosis is uncertain
serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and chest imaging to exclude sarcoidosis
autoimmune serology including antinuclear and ANCA antibodies
syphilis serology and interferon-gamma release assay
dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography for macular oedema
redFlags: acute kidney injury with a rising creatinine requiring urgent nephrology input
bilateral uveitis with systemic constitutional symptoms in an adolescent
features suggesting systemic vasculitis such as haematuria and pulmonary involvement
sight-threatening posterior involvement or persistent macular oedema
reference.prognosis: The renal component usually responds well to corticosteroids and often recovers fully, though a minority develop chronic renal impairment; the uveitis frequently follows a chronic or relapsing course and requires longer treatment than the nephritis.
pitfalls: Treating the uveitis in isolation and missing coexisting or subsequent renal disease.
Failing to measure renal function and urinary beta-2 microglobulin in a young patient with bilateral anterior uveitis.
Attributing the syndrome to a drug reaction without excluding sarcoidosis and other systemic causes.
Assuming the uveitis will resolve with the nephritis, when it commonly relapses and outlasts the renal disease.
Overlooking posterior segment involvement and chronic macular oedema as causes of persistent visual loss.
